content: Low vision during childhood poses a significant challenge to learning and development, particularly in the areas of reading and education. Optical low vision aids are tools designed to enhance the functional vision of children with visual impairments. The World Health Organization (WHO) has previously emphasized the importance of utilizing such aids to manage visual impairments in children globally. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of optical low vision aids on reading abilities in children and young people with low vision. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL (which incorporates the Cochrane Eyes and Vision Group Trials Register), Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Health Technology Assessment Programme (HTA), the ISRCTN registry, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). The search spanned from January 1946 to January 2015, with the last search performed on January 8, 2015. No restrictions were applied regarding the date or language of the studies. Additionally, manual searches of reference lists in retrieved articles were performed, and manufacturers of low vision aids were contacted to obtain any relevant research or study data. The inclusion criteria for this review were specific. It aimed to include randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared any optical low vision aid to standard refractive correction in children and young people aged 5 to 16 years with low vision, as defined by the WHO. Studies employing a within-person design, where the order of device presentation was randomized, were also considered eligible. Two independent authors reviewed the search results to determine their eligibility for inclusion. Unfortunately, no studies met the inclusion criteria for this review. As a result, there is currently a lack of high-quality evidence regarding the effectiveness of optical low vision aids in children and young people. Consequently, no definitive recommendations for clinical practice can be made based on the available data. The authors of this review emphasize the need for future research to address this gap. They recommend that future studies incorporate functional outcome measures, such as reading speed, reading accuracy, and reading comprehension, as well as assessments of the impact of low vision aids on quality of life. These measures are essential to comprehensively evaluate and compare the effects of optical low vision aids on the lives and developmental progress of children with visual impairments.
